messages.subject: standard deviation in pca
messages.body_plain:
The proportion of variation explained by PCA components is the sum of the “standard deviation” (eigenvalues) of those components divided by the sum for all components. For high-dimensional data, the eigenvalues will often be close to 0 for many components, so it’s rarely necessary to calculate all of the components.

The PCA method used to include a proportion of variance explained in its summary, but this was removed because it was being calculated incorrectly, because in practice we will frequently calculate fewer PCA than necessary to calculate the variance explained.

I simply forgot to remove that line from the vignette. Sorry about the confusion.

messages.subject: To z-standardize or not to z-standardize data for PCA
messages.subject_clean: To z-standardize or not to z-standardize data for PCA
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am dealing with MSI-data for the first time, and have been playing with a dataset, trying out different software packages. I ran Matlab's PCA algorithm on my data processed with MSiReader, and then tried out the processing and PCA in Cardinal for comparison, getting vastly different results.  I realised that the default in Cardinal is not to z-standardize the data for the PCA, whilst this is something that is generally done in my field and which I did when running the Matlab algorithm. Turning on z-standardization in Cardinal then gave me very similar results to the Matlab PCA. In my understanding, if the data are not z-standardized, the peaks with the highest mean intensity will contribute and explain more variance in the data, is this correct? It seems to be the case for my data: with the Cardinal PCA, the highest intensity peaks also have the highest standard deviation and have the strongest loadings on component 1 and there seems to be linear relationship between average peak height and component loading. So I was wondering if anybody could explain to me what is the rationale behind not z-standardizing the data. Is it that the highest peaks are likely the least noisy peaks? Or that in order to interpret the basis spectra (component spectra) better, it is better to keep the original scaling of the data? The thing I am concerned about is that if doing so, I will miss peaks that are not amongst the highest, but that are spatially very informative. I’d be grateful if I could get some input on this!

Thanks a lot,

Ilona

messages.subject: Re: Legend position in plotted images of cardinal example data
messages.subject_clean: Legend position in plotted images of cardinal example data
messages.body_plain:
For the Cardinal plots generated using base graphics, each plot is generated independently regardless of the layout, which is why each subplot has its own colorkey. This is necessary mainly so that selectROI() works properly and easily, as most of the methods that would create a single colorkey for multiple plots require creating additional plotting regions that throws off the coordinate system.

For Cardinal 1.0 classes (MSImageSet), you can switch the plotting engine from base to "lattice" by setting "lattice=TRUE". This will do what you want and automatically have a single colorkey for all plots.

For Cardinal 2.0 classes (MSImagingExperiment), lattice graphics aren't supported, but if you pass a list() of arguments to "colorkey", these arguments will be passed to the legend() function, so you can modify the placement and other legend() parameters. However, there will still be multiple colorkeys.

If you want to create a single colorkey for all plots by yourself using R code, here is some example code that would help you get started:

library(CardinalWorkflows)
data(pig206)
layout(matrix(c(1,2,3,3), nrow=2, ncol=2), widths=c(3,1))
image(pig206, mz=c(563,888), col.regions=gradient.colors(100), colorkey=FALSE)
image(matrix(1:100, nrow=1, ncol=100), col=gradient.colors(100), xaxt='n', yaxt='n')

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: Getting "out of memory" error while normalising the raw data (on a machine with 200GB RAM)
messages.subject_clean: Getting "out of memory" error while normalising the raw data (on a machine with 200GB RAM)
messages.body_plain:
The issue is that attach.only=TRUE will not load the dataset into memory, but the normalize() function returns its output in-memory, so you are producing a large in-memory matrix.

The old solution for this is that ideally you are combining normalize() with some processing steps like peakPick() that will reduce the size of the data at the same time, so that the result is smaller than the original raw data and can fit in memory. With old classes ("MSImageSet"), this is done with the batchProcess() function. See the documentation for that function and see if it may work for you.

The new solution for data imported as the new classes ("MSImagingExperiment") is that each processing step is queued and only applied later using the process() function. This would allow you to combine normalize() and peakPick() in a similar way to batchProcess(). However, an additional option with process() is the "outpath" argument which lets you specify a file path where the result will be written rather than returned it in memory. This is an option if your result will also be very large.

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: To z-standardize or not to z-standardize data for PCA
messages.subject_clean: To z-standardize or not to z-standardize data for PCA
messages.body_plain:
You are essentially correct. When you don't standardize/scale the data beforehand, PCA will be dominated by the peaks with the highest variance. This is not necessarily the ones with the highest mean intensities, but that is often the case (particularly because MS data tends to have multiplicative variance, so higher intensity peaks will usually have higher variance). This isn't necessarily undesirable, depending on whether or not you think the peaks with the highest variance will also be the most relevant.

It is essentially up to you whether to scale the data, and there is no issue with looking at both scaled and unscaled results. If you believe there may be peaks with lower intensity/variance that may contribute to whatever you are investigating, then you are correct that it would be better to scale the data.

My reasoning behind the defaults here is primarily to be consistent with other PCA implementations elsewhere in R such as the prcomp() function.

-Kylie

messages.subject_clean: Getting "out of memory" error while normalising the raw data (on a machine with 200GB RAM)
messages.body_plain:
Currently, the analytic functions (besides PCA) do not support out-of-memory data, so the data must fit in memory before applying analysis like spatialKMeans and spatialShrunkenCentroids.

The next version of Cardinal (released sometime in late April or early May -- I am still waiting on the release schedule for Bioconductor 3.9) will begin adding support for out-of-memory data in analytic functions like spatialKMeans and spatialShrunkenCentroids.

Note that either way, it is strongly recommended to reduce the dimension of the data (e.g., through peak-picking) before doing statistical analysis.
